questions.q: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with generalized granuloma annulare presenting with widespread annular lesions over his trunk and extremities. Which systemic associations are most commonly reported with the generalized variant compared to the localized form?
opts: Hypothyroidism alone, without dyslipidemia or glucose intolerance
Diabetes mellitus (21% incidence) and dyslipidemia, with increased risk warranting metabolic screening
Exclusively lymphoproliferative malignancies with 100% predictive value for Hodgkin's lymphoma
Tuberculosis and fungal infections as the primary systemic associations
questions.exp: Generalized GA (GGA) shows a significantly increased incidence of diabetes mellitus (21% compared to 10% in localized forms) and elevated prevalence of dyslipidemia, making metabolic evaluation important in these patients. While thyroid disease and malignancy associations have been reported, the most consistent and relevant screening involves glucose and lipid assessment.

questions.q: A newborn girl has a congenital haemangioma that is GLUT1-negative and carries a somatic GNAQ Gln209 mutation. Which of the following statements regarding the pathogenesis and epidemiology of congenital haemangiomas is CORRECT?
opts: Congenital haemangiomas show a strong female predominance similar to infantile haemangiomas
The Gln209 mutation constitutively upregulates the MAPK pathway and drives prenatal tumour growth
All congenital haemangiomas complete their involution by 6 months of postnatal life regardless of subtype
GLUT1-positive immunostaining reliably differentiates congenital from infantile haemangiomas
questions.exp: The GNAQ/GNA11 Gln209 mutation constitutively activates the MAPK pathway, driving prenatal proliferation and completion of growth *in utero*. Unlike infantile haemangiomas, congenital haemangiomas affect males and females equally, and GLUT1 negativity (not positivity) is the distinguishing marker. Involution timelines vary by subtype (RICH ~14 months, NICH never, PICH partial).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a GNAQ KNIGHT in the castle MAPK throne room, constantly PUMPING MITOGEN FUEL into the prenatal FURNACE—the mutation is a perpetual IGNITION switch lit *before birth*, so the tumour arrives FULLY FORMED and GLUT1-DARK (negative).

questions.q: A 3-week-old presents with fever, irritability, and extreme cutaneous tenderness followed by orange-red macules with flexural accentuation. Within 48 hours, tissue-paper-like wrinkling progresses over the trunk and limbs. Blood culture and skin culture are both positive for Staphylococcus aureus. Histopathology shows subcorneal acantholysis but WITHOUT neutrophilic infiltrate in the blister cavity. What is the key pathophysiological difference between this condition and localized bullous impetigo?
opts: The toxin cleaves desmoglein 3 instead of desmoglein 1
Exfoliative toxins diffuse systemically from an occult primary infection focus rather than acting locally
The primary pathogen is Streptococcus pyogenes instead of Staphylococcus aureus
The cleavage plane is suprabasal rather than subcorneal
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS, Ritter's disease) differs from localized bullous impetigo in that the exfoliative toxins (particularly ETB) disseminate hematogenously from a distant, often occult primary focus of infection (e.g., omphalitis or conjunctivitis) rather than acting locally at the site of bacterial inoculation. Both conditions target Dsg1 and cause subcorneal cleavage, but the distribution and systemic nature distinguish SSSS as the generalized form.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a POISON GAS CLOUD (systemic toxin) leaking from a distant factory (omphalitis in the belly) and spreading across an entire kingdom (whole body), versus a LOCAL SPILL (bullous impetigo) at the warehouse door affecting only one corner.

questions.q: A 1-day-old neonate presents with generalized erythroderma, superficial blistering, and erosions. Histopathology reveals prominent vacuolar degeneration of suprabasal and granular layers with dense keratin intermediate filament clumps and orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis. Which genetic defect is most likely responsible?
opts: Mutations in ALOX12B or ALOXE3 affecting lipid processing
Mutations in KRT1 or KRT10 affecting keratin intermediate filaments
Mutations in SPINK5 causing loss of protease inhibition
Mutations in filaggrin (FLG) predisposing to atopic dermatitis
questions.exp: Epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI) is characterized by mutations in KRT1 and KRT10 genes encoding keratin structural proteins. The pathognomonic histopathologic finding is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration of suprabasal layers, cytolysis, and characteristic keratin clumping. This autosomal dominant condition presents at birth with erythroderma and superficial blistering that resolves into flexural hyperkeratosis by late infancy.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine KERATIN KNIGHTS (KRT1/KRT10) marching through the SUPRABASAL CASTLE HALLWAY, leaving CLUMPS OF ARMOR (keratin filaments) and VACUOUS HOLES (cytolysis) as they collapse—the hallmark fingerprint of EI's epidermolytic chaos.

questions.q: A 32-week-gestation female infant is born prematurely to parents from a South Dakota Hutterite community with a history of polyhydramnios and decreased fetal movements. The infant has severe skin tightness and dies within 5 days from respiratory insufficiency. Which of the following statements about restrictive dermopathy epidemiology and inheritance in this population is CORRECT?
opts: The condition shows clear female predominance and HLA associations with specific serotypes
A shared founder mutation is highly prevalent in Hutterite and Old Colony Mennonite populations, with carrier frequencies estimated up to 1 in 21
The disease typically follows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance across ethnic groups
Restrictive dermopathy occurs exclusively in populations of North American indigenous descent
questions.exp: Restrictive dermopathy shows no sex bias and has no HLA associations because it is a Mendelian monogenic laminopathy. A specific shared founder mutation is exceptionally prevalent in Hutterite and Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite populations in North America, with carrier frequencies as high as 1 in 21 in South Dakota Hutterites. The classical (ZMPSTE24-mutated) form follows autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.q: A 3-month-old female infant born at 28 weeks gestation presents with a rapidly enlarging red nodule on the cheek that was not present at birth but appeared within the first 2 weeks of life. Immunohistochemistry reveals diffuse GLUT1 positivity throughout the lesion. Which of the following best explains the biological nature of this lesion?
opts: A vascular malformation composed of dysplastic, quiescent endothelial cells
A true benign vascular neoplasm characterized by active endothelial hyperplasia and proliferation
A congenital hemangioma with involutional capacity beginning at birth
A hamartomatous malformation with no propensity for spontaneous regression
questions.exp: Infantile haemangiomas are true benign vascular neoplasms—not structural malformations—defined by active endothelial hyperplasia. The GLUT1 glucose transporter is the universal hallmark expressed throughout all phases (proliferating, involuting, involuted), definitively distinguishing IH from vascular malformations and congenital haemangiomas. This patient's early postnatal onset and rapid proliferation are typical of IH.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a NEOPLASTIC KNIGHT on his horse GALLOPING through the castle at full speed (proliferating), carrying a GLUT1-marked shield that NEVER FADES, even as he slows to a trot (involuting) and finally stops (involuted)—the shield remains branded on him forever.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 14 weeks gestation is diagnosed with primary syphilis. What is the approximate transmission risk to the fetus, and what single intervention would most likely prevent fetal infection and irreversible stigmata?
opts: 40% risk; adequate penicillin treatment before 16–18 weeks almost always prevents fetal infection
70–100% risk; adequate penicillin treatment before 16–18 weeks almost always prevents fetal infection
10% risk; maternal treatment after delivery prevents neonatal complications
70–100% risk; penicillin treatment in the third trimester is most effective
questions.exp: Primary syphilis in pregnancy carries a 70–100% transmission risk. The fetus does not achieve full immunocompetence until 18–20 weeks gestation, meaning adequate penicillin treatment before the 16–18 week threshold almost always prevents fetal infection and irreversible stigmata. Early maternal treatment is the cornerstone of prevention.
questions.mem: 🏰 Palace: Picture a PREGNANT WOMAN at week 14 standing at the GATES of a castle labeled '16–18 WEEKS.' A giant PENICILLIN SWORD destroys the spirochetes BEFORE they cross the placental moat—but the sword becomes useless after the gates close. Kassowitz's Law: the LONGER the delay before pregnancy, the GENTLER the disease.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from Brazil presents with a 2-year history of progressive nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and palatal ulceration. He recalls a solitary cutaneous lesion on his leg that healed completely 3 years ago. Which immunopathological mechanism best explains the severe mucosal destruction in mucocutaneous leishmaniasis?
opts: T-cell anergy and specific tolerance to the parasite, allowing unrestricted parasitic proliferation
Exaggerated Th1-mediated cellular hypersensitivity with massive pro-inflammatory cytokine production causing autoimmune tissue destruction
Humoral immune deficiency leading to impaired opsonization and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
Direct parasitic invasion and multiplication in mucosal tissues without significant host immune involvement
questions.exp: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL) is pathophysiologically driven by a hyperergic Th1 response with excessive TNF-alpha and pro-inflammatory cytokine production that destroys host tissue in an attempt to clear sparse parasites. This is the opposite of diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL), which results from T-cell anergy and tolerance. The intense, uncontrolled inflammation is responsible for the characteristic mucosal destruction and 'tapir nose' deformity.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FURIOUS KNIGHT (Th1) in the castle destroying his OWN WALLS with FLAMING TORCHES (TNF-alpha) to kill ONE HIDDEN MOUSE (sparse parasite) in the corner—MCL is self-inflicted immune warfare, not parasite power.

questions.q: A newborn presents with profoundly rigid, tightly adherent skin and severe restriction of chest wall expansion leading to respiratory insufficiency. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. What is the primary consequence of ZMPSTE24 deficiency in restrictive dermopathy?
opts: Loss of direct lamin A and C structural proteins in the nuclear envelope
Failure to cleave and process farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A, causing toxic accumulation at the nuclear lamina
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of dermal collagen fibers via HLA-associated mechanisms
Impaired post-translational modification of elastin in the dermal extracellular matrix
questions.exp: ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase responsible for the essential post-translational cleavage of farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A. Without this enzyme, unprocessed toxic prelamin A accumulates at the nuclear lamina, distorting nuclear structure and arresting skin maturation during the second trimester. This represents the most common (secondary laminopathy) form of restrictive dermopathy.

questions.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with flaccid bullae (1–2 cm) on the diaper area that ruptured within 24 hours, leaving thin golden-yellow crusts with a peripheral collarette of scale. The Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. Gram-positive cocci are cultured from the blister fluid. Which desmosomal protein is the primary target of the exfoliative toxin in this condition?
opts: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Desmocollin 1 (Dsc1)
E-cadherin
questions.exp: In bullous impetigo of the newborn, exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) produced by Staphylococcus aureus act as trypsin-like serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), a desmosomal cadherin responsible for superficial epidermal adhesion. This causes subcorneal/subgranular acantholysis characteristic of localized bullous impetigo.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture Dsg1 as a GOLD CHAIN dangling from a newborn's crib; the toxin SNIPS the chain like scissors, and golden crusts fall to the nursery floor below.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) caused by Leishmania donovani presents with ashy-gray to black hyperpigmentation of the face, temples, and abdomen. Which statement correctly links the clinical presentation to the pathophysiology of this disease?
opts: Melanin is directly produced by parasitized melanocytes in the epidermis, resulting in localized pigmentation

The diffuse hyperpigmentation reflects widespread reticuloendothelial system involvement with secondary stimulation of melanin synthesis, earning the disease its Hindi name 'Kala-azar' meaning 'Black Sickness'
Hemolysis from parasitic destruction of red blood cells releases hemoglobin, which is converted to melanin-like pigments in the dermis
Chronic immune complex deposition in the basement membrane triggers melanin overproduction as a protective response
questions.exp: Visceral leishmaniasis predominantly affects the reticuloendothelial system, and the hallmark cutaneous sign is diffuse ashy-gray to black hyperpigmentation on the face, temples, abdomen, and extremities. This striking pigmentary change directly inspired the Hindi name 'Kala-azar' (Black Sickness). The hyperpigmentation represents secondary melanin stimulation from systemic reticuloendothelial involvement rather than direct parasitic invasion of skin.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a DARK SHADOW spreading across the entire CASTLE as the KING'S DARK TREASURY (reticuloendothelial system) fails—the whole kingdom turns BLACK (Kala-azar) from systemic disease, not local paint.

questions.q: A full-term neonate is born encased in a shiny, taut membrane that gradually sheds over the first weeks of life, leaving fine white feathery scales and persistent generalized erythroderma. Ectropion and palmoplantar keratoderma are noted. Which inheritance pattern and molecular defect characterize this condition?
opts: Autosomal dominant; mutations in KRT1/KRT10 affecting keratin intermediate filaments
Autosomal recessive; mutations in lipid-processing genes (ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, CERS3, TGM1)
Autosomal recessive; mutations in SPINK5 causing unregulated stratum corneum desquamation
X-linked recessive; mutations affecting tight junction proteins
questions.exp: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE) is an autosomal recessive condition in the ARCI spectrum caused by defects in lipid processing and transport genes. The pathognomonic presentation is a collodion membrane at birth that sheds to reveal erythroderma with fine feathery scales. Ectropion, eclabium, cicatricial alopecia, and palmoplantar keratoderma are characteristic associated features distinguishing it from other ichthyoses.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A newborn PRINCE wrapped in a SHINY PLASTIC COLLODION CLOAK (lipid defect) arrives at the castle gates; once the cloak peels away, he's draped in WHITE FEATHERY SCALES and TURNED-OUT LIPS (ectropion/eclabium) for life—ARCI's signature entrance.

questions.q: A 1-week-old premature male infant presents with rapidly progressive, diffuse, board-like induration of the skin starting on the buttocks and spreading to the trunk and extremities. The skin is cold, rock-hard, and non-pitting with yellowish-white coloration and purplish mottling. Histopathology shows fat necrosis with minimal inflammation and characteristic doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of adipose tissue triggered by neonatal pathogens
Crystallization and solidification of subcutaneous fat due to high saturated fatty acid content and peripheral circulatory collapse in a physiologically stressed premature infant
Vasculitis-induced ischemic necrosis of adipose lobules secondary to septicemia
Enzymatic lipolysis triggered by immature neonatal lipase activity in response to hypothermia
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum results from the unique composition of neonatal fat—which has a high ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids—combined with severe physiological stress (sepsis, hypothermia, hypoxia) causing peripheral circulatory collapse and skin cooling. The immature enzymatic lipolytic mechanisms cannot mobilize fat for heat, leading to rapid crystallization. The pathognomonic histological finding of doubly refractile clefts represents dissolved triglyceride crystals, not inflammatory or vasculitic changes.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: A neonatal screening program identifies infantile haemangiomas in premature infants stratified by birth weight. Which birth weight category shows an incidence of infantile haemangiomas approaching 25–30%?
opts: Birth weight 1500–2000 g
Birth weight 1000–1500 g
Birth weight <1000 g
Birth weight 2000–2500 g
questions.exp: The incidence of infantile haemangiomas rises inversely with decreasing birth weight, and the most severely premature infants—those weighing less than 1000 g—show a remarkable incidence of 25–30%. A birth weight below 2500 g is an independent risk factor, and this extremely low birth weight group represents the highest-risk population.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine TINY PREMATURE BABIES in the castle nursery, each weighing LESS THAN A KILO (1000g), and 1 out of every 3 to 4 of them is COVERED IN RED SPOTS like a measles outbreak—that's the devastating 25–30% prevalence—while heavier babies are safer.

questions.q: Which of the following anatomical sites is characteristically SPARED in sclerema neonatorum, despite the diffuse, widespread encasement of subcutaneous tissues?
opts: Buttocks and thighs
Chest and abdomen
Palms, soles, and genitalia
Face and neck
questions.exp: In sclerema neonatorum, the rigid induration and board-like skin encase almost the entire body, but the palms, soles, and genitalia are characteristically spared—a clinically important distinguishing feature. This sparing may relate to differences in local perfusion or fat composition in these specialized areas.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: Genome-wide association studies in vitiligo patients have identified approximately 50 susceptibility loci. What is the approximate distribution of these loci in terms of their functional categories?
opts: 90% related to melanocyte antigens and stress-response pathways; 10% to innate and adaptive immunity
90% related to innate and adaptive immunity; 10% to melanocyte antigens and stress-response pathways
50% related to pigmentation genes; 50% to infectious disease resistance
80% related to DNA repair pathways; 20% to metabolic dysfunction
questions.exp: GWAS studies in vitiligo have identified approximately 50 susceptibility loci, with approximately 90% related to innate and adaptive immunity and 10% related to melanocyte antigens and stress-response pathways. This distribution underscores the predominant role of immune dysregulation in vitiligo pathogenesis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes excision of a facial nevus. To optimize cosmetic outcome and minimize scar widening, which layer of closure is most critical for bearing the tensile load of the wound?
opts: Epidermal layer closed with non-absorbable monofilament
Deep dermal or subcutaneous layer using absorbable buried sutures with inverted knots
Superficial running subcuticular sutures for fine alignment
Compression dressing applied immediately post-operatively
questions.exp: The deep dermal/subcutaneous layer with buried absorbable sutures (e.g., Vicryl or PDS) bears the primary tensile load, supports the wound during remodeling, and allows early removal of superficial sutures. This layered approach is fundamental to reducing tension across the wound, which is the most important determinant of final scar quality. Tension reduction prevents widened, hypertrophic, or keloid scars.

questions.q: A mother with a history of recurrent genital herpes delivers vaginally at term without active lesions. What is the approximate risk of neonatal HSV transmission in this scenario?
opts: Less than 1% to 3%
questions.exp: Mothers with recurrent genital herpes at delivery have a much lower transmission risk of less than 1% to 3%, compared to primary infection near delivery (30-50% risk). This is because recurrent infection is accompanied by protective transplacental maternal antibodies and lower viral shedding.

questions.q: A 4-week-old neonate presents with profuse, watery nasal discharge that has become purulent and blood-tinged, along with a generalized coppery-red maculopapular rash affecting the palms and soles with characteristic desquamation. Which of the following clinical findings would distinguish this presentation from acquired secondary syphilis in adults?
opts: Presence of hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy
Development of syphilitic pemphigus with vesiculobullous lesions predominantly on the palms and soles
Occurrence of snuffles (syphilitic rhinitis) as the first symptom
Appearance of condylomata lata in intertriginous areas
questions.exp: Syphilitic pemphigus is a unique feature of early congenital syphilis, presenting as a vesiculobullous eruption (blisters) often present at birth or shortly thereafter, predominantly on the palms and soles. This distinguishes congenital from acquired syphilis. While snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, and condylomata lata occur in both early congenital syphilis and secondary syphilis, the pemphigus with its characteristic palmoplantar blistering is uniquely prominent in the congenital form.
questions.mem: 🏰 Palace: In the NEWBORN's throne room, PURPLE BLISTERS bloom on PALMS and SOLES like royal jewels—this PEMPHIGUS CROWN is ONLY worn by congenital babies, never by adult secondary syphilis sufferers. The baby is a UNIQUELY SPECIAL kingdom.

questions.q: Which of the following accurately describes the developmental cycle of Chlamydia trachomatis and the role of each morphological form?
opts: The elementary body (EB) is metabolically active and replicates by binary fission within host cell vacuoles
The reticulate body (RB) is the infectious extracellular form measuring 0.3–1.0 μm with a rigid cell wall
The elementary body (EB) is the infectious extracellular form; the reticulate body (RB) is the metabolically active intracellular form that replicates by binary fission
Both EB and RB are equally infectious and can both replicate outside the host cell on chlamydial media
questions.exp: Chlamydia trachomatis exhibits a biphasic developmental cycle lasting 48–72 hours. The elementary body (EB) is the infectious, metabolically inert extracellular form (0.3–1.0 μm) that enters the host cell via endocytosis, then differentiates into the larger, metabolically active reticulate body (RB), which replicates by binary fission within a membrane-bound vacuole. After 8–12 replication cycles, RBs condense back into EBs that are released to infect adjacent cells.

questions.q: A neonate presents at 10 days of life with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the scalp at the site of a fetal scalp monitor electrode. Examination reveals keratoconjunctivitis and ulcerative stomatitis, but normal neurologic examination and no organomegaly. Which classification of neonatal HSV does this clinical presentation most clearly represent?
opts: Congenital intrauterine HSV infection
Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease
Disseminated HSV infection
CNS HSV infection
questions.exp: SEM disease presents between days 1-2 weeks of life (classically days 9-11) with grouped vesicles on erythematous bases at sites of delivery trauma or iatrogenic injury, plus keratoconjunctivitis and ulcerative stomatitis, while the CNS and visceral organs remain uninvolved. The normal neurologic exam and absence of organomegaly exclude disseminated or CNS disease.

questions.q: A 2-week-old male infant presents with a fully formed, exophytic red-violaceous nodule on the thigh that was present at birth. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with GLUT1-negative immunostaining. Genetic testing reveals a somatic GNAQ Gln209 mutation. The lesion begins to regress by 6 weeks of age and is nearly resolved by 14 months, leaving behind atrophic, hypopigmented skin. Which subtype of congenital haemangioma best describes this clinical course?
opts: Rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH)
Non-involuting congenital haemangioma (NICH)
Partially involuting congenital haemangioma (PICH)
Infantile haemangioma with somatic mutation
questions.exp: RICH undergoes swift postnatal regression beginning within days to weeks of birth, with complete involution typically by 14 months, and frequently leaves residual atrophic, hypopigmented skin. The GLUT1-negative status, somatic GNAQ mutation, and presence at birth distinguish this from infantile haemangioma, while the rapid involution rules out NICH (which persists) and PICH (which shows partial regression).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a RICH baby RAPIDLY RACING out of the castle nursery by 14 months, leaving behind RAGGED RAGS (atrophic skin) on the floor—RICH = RAPID Regression by 14-month deadline.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with progressive, sharply demarcated milky-white patches on her face and hands over the past 6 months. She has a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Which pathogenic mechanism is most strongly implicated in her vitiligo based on current evidence?
opts: T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of melanocytes with CD8+ T cell infiltration and IFN-γ-mediated signaling
Fungal colonization of the epidermis leading to melanocyte senescence
Purely genetic mutation in the MC1R receptor gene causing loss of melanin synthesis
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide-induced apoptosis of basal keratinocytes
questions.exp: The autoimmune theory is the most plausible pathogenic mechanism in vitiligo, supported by the association with other autoimmune diseases like Hashimoto thyroiditis and by GWAS data showing ~90% of susceptibility loci are immune-related. Activated CD8+ T cells infiltrate perilesional skin and generate type 1 cytokines, with IFN-γ and CXCL10 playing critical roles in melanocyte destruction via JAK-STAT1 signaling through keratinocyte IFN-γR.

questions.q: A surgeon is deciding between octyl cyanoacrylate (Dermabond) and buried dermal sutures for closing a 3 cm laceration under moderate tension on the forearm of a 6-year-old child. Which statement accurately reflects the contraindications of tissue adhesives in this scenario?
opts: Cyanoacrylate is ideal for this wound because it polymerizes rapidly and children tolerate it better than sutures
Cyanoacrylate should not be used because the wound is under significant tension and requires deep tensile support that sutures provide
Cyanoacrylate is contraindicated only for mucosal surfaces, making it safe for all skin wounds
Cyanoacrylate can be used as an internal deep suture if mixed with fibrin glue to reduce toxicity
questions.exp: Tissue adhesives are explicitly contraindicated for wounds under significant tension because they lack the tensile strength and cannot provide the deep structural support needed. While cyanoacrylate has bacteriostatic properties and rapid setting, it is also absolutely contraindicated for internal/subcutaneous placement due to toxic degradation byproducts (cyanoacetate and formaldehyde) causing tissue necrosis and inflammation. In this case, layered closure with buried dermal sutures is required.

questions.q: A 32-year-old MSM presents with severe proctocolitis and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Rectal biopsy and PCR confirm Chlamydia trachomatis L2b serovar. Which characteristic of the L1–L3 serovars distinguishes them pathogenically from serovars D–K?
opts: They are strictly epitheliotropic and cause only urethritis
They are invasive and lymphotropic, penetrating beyond mucosa and triggering regional lymphadenitis via macrophage transport
They replicate exclusively in the reticulate body form within epithelial cells
They cannot form infectious elementary bodies and therefore require continuous reinfection
questions.exp: The L1–L3 serovars causing LGV are invasive and lymphotropic, penetrating the mucosa through microscopic abrasions and being transported by macrophages to regional lymph nodes where they trigger severe inflammation and characteristic stellate abscesses. In contrast, serovars D–K are strictly epitheliotropic, causing only superficial mucosal infections such as urethritis or cervicitis. The distinction in tissue tropism is fundamental to LGV's pathogenesis and clinical presentation of severe regional lymphadenitis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with a chronic, non-pruritic annular erythematous lesion on her dorsal hand that has been present for 6 months. Histopathology reveals granulomatous inflammation with necrobiosis. Which of the following best characterizes the immune mechanism proposed in granuloma annulare?
opts: IgE-mediated Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation
Delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction with T-cell-mediated macrophage activation and cytokine-mediated connective tissue degradation
Antibody-mediated immune complex deposition with complement activation
Direct cytotoxic T-cell killing of infected keratinocytes
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare is postulated to be a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to an unknown antigen, with T-cell repertoire studies demonstrating T-cell-mediated macrophage activation. Cytokines including TNF-α, interferon-gamma, and IL-2 drive cytokine-mediated degradation of connective tissue, distinguishing it from other hypersensitivity mechanisms.
